info.desc: Low is the eleventh studio album by British musician David Bowie, co-produced by Bowie and Tony Visconti. Widely regarded as one of Bowie's most influential releases, Low was the first of the "Berlin Trilogy", a series of collaborations with Brian Eno (though the album was mainly recorded in France and only mixed in West Berlin). The experimental, avant-garde style would be further explored on "Heroes" and Lodger. The album's working title was New Music Night and Day. The genesis of Low lies in both the foundations laid by Bowie's previous album Station to Station, and music he intended for the .

podcast.body: Despite Bowie's refusal to change the album and RCA's initial reservations, "Low" was released as he intended and achieved significant critical and commercial success. It was considered an "instant classic" upon release and performed surprisingly well in sales, exceeding expectations for its experimental and risky nature, although it did not reach the monumental chart positions of his previous "grand hits." Bowie himself was reportedly surprised by its success.

podcast.body: Recorded at Hansa Studio in Berlin, this album was experimental and often very electronic, reflecting Bowie's fascination with German electronic music, specifically Kraftwerk. It was a colder-sounding record, made while Bowie was trying desperately to kick his cocaine addiction and experiencing physical and psychic pain. Side 1 featured short song fragments (none longer than 3.5 minutes), while Side 2 was entirely instrumental and included significant contributions from Brian Eno. Initially confusing to critics, it later became recognized as a bold work that expanded the reach of synthesizer music beyond its German origins, influencing post-punk bands like Joy Division. "Low, an experimental and often very electronic album that was part man who fell to earth, part station to station and part whatever was happening in Berlin at the time."

podcast.body: Recorded in 1976 and released in 1977, this was the initial album of Bowie's Berlin Trilogy, though most of its recording did not take place in Berlin, nor with "Dayan." The album came together from numerous unfinished or rejected projects, including outtakes from "Station to Station," an abandoned soundtrack for "The Man Who Fell to Earth," and material from "Honky Dory." Recording sessions occurred in Los Angeles, his personal studio in Geneva, and Paris, with Berlin primarily serving as a place for idea development. Musically, it incorporated influences from German Krautrock artists like Kraftwerk, Neu!, and Cluster, despite lacking direct lyrical references to Berlin.

podcast.body: The album's credits were minimal, with Bowie appearing almost in solo. Brian Eno was credited for some songs and production, but not as a composer for many of his contributions. This led to controversy, as many uncredited artists who were part of the creative and recording process claimed involvement. This lack of clear attribution was likely due to the dispersed recording across multiple locations over a long period, changing personnel, and Bowie's struggles with addiction at the time, making it difficult for him to track who participated.

podcast.body: The album's release was delayed until 1977 due to problems Bowie encountered with both his current and former managers who still had financial interests. RCA initially refused to release the album, not considering it a guaranteed success despite Bowie's track record of producing chart-topping hits. The label suggested Bowie rework the album with more commercially appealing tracks.

podcast.body: This album, Bowie's 11th, was recorded at Château d'Hérouville with producer Tony Visconti and the core band of Carlos Alomar, George Murray, and Dennis Davis. Initially, Bowie was not entirely satisfied with the sound, leading him to invite Brian Eno to join the recording sessions. Bowie considered it a very special, melancholic album reflecting his mental recovery, thus believing it wouldn't be commercially successful. He refused to promote it, choosing instead to tour as a keyboardist for Iggy Pop, aiming to stay in the background. Despite initial mixed reviews, it performed quite well commercially. "En lausa respira melancolía, Bowie lo considera muy especial, grabado en una época de recuperación mental donde plasmoso estado, por lo que creía que no iba a funcionar comercialmente."
